title: Computer Organisation
summary: How a computer works from the transistor up: logic gates and circuits, number formats, instruction sets, the processor's datapath and control, I/O, memory and caches, pipelining, parallelism and virtual memory. Alongside the lectures you program in x86-64 assembly in the lab. The grade is a points game: two exams of 4000 points each plus points from bonus labs, self-study, quizzes and tutorials, divided by 1000.

basis.description: Slides of Lectures 0 to 15 as text, the 2024-25 lab manual, the self-study sets for weeks 2 to 9, and six exam papers from 2023-24 and 2024-25 with rubrics. Time shares count content slides; Lecture 0 (course organisation) and the lab introduction slides in Lecture 2 are left out.
basis.caveat: From 2026-27 the course is CSE11C, renamed from CSE1400, in year 1, quarter 1; the curriculum note says the content is unchanged. The slides show one combined Lecture 15, while the official schedule lists superscalar execution and parallel and virtual memory as two lectures. The memory lecture is mostly figures without text, so its share here is on the low side.

topics.name: History of computing
know: The pre-history: mechanical calculators, the [[Jacquard loom as the first programmable machine]], Babbage's Difference and Analytical Engines, and [[Ada Lovelace as the first programmer]]
Electro-mechanical and early electronic machines (ASCC/Harvard Mark I, ENIAC) and the practical problems that made them hard to use: size, power, failing valves, rewiring to reprogram
Atanasoff's digital computer, the [[stored-program (Von Neumann) idea]], the transistor, the microprocessor and the IBM PC
The multi-computing generation: networked machines and the roots of the Internet
Rough dates of landmarks such as the first computer bug, the mouse, the Apple computer and the Internet
Why war and military funding sped up computing, and why performance is the thread through the whole history
do: Put a list of inventions in chronological order
Name problems of early machines and explain in a sentence or two why each mattered
pitfalls: Naming the problems without saying why they were significant: on the 2025 midterm the explanation part was worth more than the list itself

topics.name: Assembly programming (x86-64)
know: The x86-64 general-purpose registers, their 32, 16 and 8-bit partial names, and the instruction [[suffixes b, w, l and q for operand size]]
AT&T syntax ([[source first, destination second]]) versus Intel syntax, and the addressing modes: immediate, register, direct, indirect and base plus offset
The stack: push and pop, how %rsp moves, and how call and ret save and follow the return address
Stack frames: the prologue ([[push %rbp, then copy %rsp to %rbp]]), local variables at negative offsets from %rbp, and the epilogue
The System V calling convention: [[arguments in %rdi, %rsi, %rdx, %rcx, %r8, %r9]], then on the stack; [[the return value in %rax]]; callee-saved versus caller-saved registers
Why the stack must be [[16-byte aligned before calling a C function]] such as printf or scanf
Assembler directives (.text, .data, .bss, .quad, .asciz, .global) and conditional jumps for if-then-else and loops
do: Trace a short subroutine and draw the stack contents after each push, call and store
Find what a piece of uncommented assembly computes and spot the bug in it
Write a recursive subroutine such as factorial or Fibonacci that respects the calling convention
Work out what an unaligned stack or a missing pop does to the values a program uses
pitfalls: Forgetting that the pushed %rbp and the return address also sit on the stack when you draw it
Losing track of bytes that were never written: an unaligned or unbalanced stack leaves unknown values that the code then reads

topics.name: Logic circuits and Boolean algebra
know: The Boolean algebra laws, including De Morgan, and how a truth table becomes a sum of products
The gates AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR and XOR, and why [[NAND and NOR are universal]]
Karnaugh maps for four variables: [[Gray-code order, wrap-around groups, corners and don't-cares]], and how they give a minimal sum of products
CMOS gates: [[PMOS transistors in the pull-up network, NMOS in the pull-down network]], and why this uses almost no power compared with resistors
Propagation delay and transition time in networks of gates
Building blocks: half and full adder, multiplexer, SR latch, gated latch, D flip-flop, shift register, counter
Combinational versus sequential circuits and the role of the clock
Moore's law and Rock's law
do: Fill a Karnaugh map from a verbal specification, including don't-cares, and read off the minimal sum of products
Prove that two expressions or circuits are equivalent with a truth table or the algebra laws
Draw the pull-up and pull-down network for a given function, or give the transistor states and output of a given CMOS circuit
Design a small circuit from AND, OR and NOT gates, or with multiplexers, from a truth table
Find and fix the mistake in a given circuit such as a full adder
pitfalls: Missing the corner group or a lone 1 that has to be circled as its own term: the Midterm 2025 rubric gave separate points for each
Drawing a resistor instead of a PMOS pull-up network, or far more transistors than needed: the Resit 2023 rubric gave partial or no points for these

topics.name: Data representation
know: Positional number systems and converting between radices by largest power or by repeated division, and the shortcut between radix 2, 4, 8 and 16 by grouping bits
Unsigned binary and BCD
Signed formats: [[sign and magnitude, one's complement, two's complement and excess-x (biased)]], with the range and the zeros of each
Sign extension, and addition and overflow detection in each signed format, including the [[end-around carry in one's complement]]
Fixed-point fractions and converting a decimal fraction to binary
IEEE 754 single precision: [[sign bit, 8-bit exponent with bias 127, 23-bit mantissa with a hidden bit]], and how custom formats change these widths and the bias
The trade-off between fixed and floating point: [[range against precision]]
do: Convert numbers between radices, including odd ones such as radix 4, 7, 12 and 36, showing every step
Decode a mix of BCD, sign and magnitude, one's complement, two's complement and excess-x values and add them up
Subtract in two's complement by [[adding the negated number and dropping the carry]]
Encode a decimal number in a custom floating-point format with a given exponent bias, and decode one back
Work out the largest, smallest or lost precision of a format after bits are removed
pitfalls: Adding the carry back in when subtracting in two's complement: the end-around carry belongs to one's complement, and the Midterm 2025 rubric gave only part of the points for it
Forgetting the range of the target format: a positive sum such as 160 no longer fits in 8-bit two's complement and reads as a negative number
Writing only the result: conversions without the intermediate steps lose points, even when the answer is right

topics.name: Instruction set architectures
know: Memory organisation from the ISA's point of view: byte and word addressability, alignment, and big versus little endian
Three, two, one and zero-address instructions, and how each handles an expression
[[Accumulator, stack, register-memory and register-register]] architectures
Addressing modes: [[immediate, direct, register, indirect and index]], and what each costs in instruction bits
CISC versus RISC characteristics (and the extreme of MISC), with the arguments for and against each, including the frequency of instruction use
How the bits of an instruction are split between opcode, register fields, memory addresses and immediate values
do: Write the code for an expression in a zero-address ISA via postfix notation, and in a two or three-address ISA
Count the minimum number of instructions an expression needs in a given ISA
Compute how many opcodes fit, given the instruction length, the number of registers and the memory size
Argue which of hardware designer, compiler writer or programmer carries the burden in a given ISA style
pitfalls: Getting the bits for a memory operand wrong: count them from the memory size and whether it is byte or word addressable
Listing extra advantages or disadvantages that are wrong: the rubrics take points off for incorrect additional statements

topics.name: Basic processing unit and control
know: Instruction execution in stages: [[fetch, decode and operand fetch, execute, write back]]
The single-bus CISC-style BPU and the RISC-style BPU, and the registers [[PC, IR, MAR, MDR, X, Y and Z]]
Tri-state gates on the bus, the register file with RF in and RF out, and which bus connections are one-way
Control signals such as [[PC out, MAR in, READ, WMFC and END]], and the step counter that sequences them
Hardwired control versus microprogrammed control: the control store in ROM, microinstructions and microroutines
Horizontal versus vertical encoding of microinstructions and how many bits each needs
How waiting for memory (WMFC and MFC) stops the step counter
do: Write the shortest microroutine for a given instruction, including the instruction fetch
Read a table of control bits and say what the microroutine does
Count the clock ticks or bus steps an instruction takes
Compute the number of control bits for a horizontally or vertically encoded microinstruction
Explain why a CISC instruction with a memory operand cannot be one RISC instruction
pitfalls: Confusing microinstructions with machine instructions, which the 2025 endterm rubric penalised
Swapping the meaning of horizontal and vertical encoding
Leaving out the fetch steps or the END signal from a microroutine

topics.name: Input/output and interrupts
know: Bus topology and the bus interface: address decoding, memory-mapped I/O, and what happens when address lines are ignored
Synchronous buses (including multi-cycle transfers) and asynchronous buses with handshake signals
Program-controlled I/O with polling, as in the video terminal example
Interrupts: the execution flow, the interrupt service routine, and the cost of the extra work
Handling several devices: [[polling, vectored interrupts, priorities and daisy chaining]] of the grant line
Direct memory access: why it is needed, what the DMA controller does, and how it affects [[throughput rather than latency]]
do: Work out which addresses a device answers to when some address lines are not connected
Add up IRQ response, grant forwarding and ISR times along a daisy chain and decide whether every device is served in time
Compute the time to send data over a synchronous bus at a given clock rate
Choose between polling, interrupts and DMA for a described device
pitfalls: Getting the daisy-chain sum wrong: [[count the CPU's grant delay once, then one forwarding delay for each device]] up to and including the one being served
Giving bus transfer times in the wrong unit when the question asks for nanoseconds

topics.name: Memory organisation
know: How one bit is stored: the [[SRAM cell of cross-coupled transistors with a word line and two bit lines]]
Memory arrays split into rows and columns, and the row and column address pins this needs
The cost of a memory chip in pins: [[address, data and control lines]]
How the number of address lines relates to word size and byte addressability
Building larger memories from smaller chips
Interleaved versus flat memory banks, and which address bits select the bank in each
do: Fill in the missing size, address pins or data pins of a memory chip from a figure
Compute how many chips of a given size a memory needs and how they are arranged
Pick the bank-select bits for an interleaved layout, after the bits for the byte within a word
Draw an SRAM cell and explain how it keeps its value once the word line is low
pitfalls: Forgetting the byte-offset bits within a word when you choose the bank bits for interleaving

topics.name: Caches and virtual memory
know: The memory hierarchy and why caches work: [[temporal and spatial locality]]
Average access time [[c + (1 - h) m]], with hit ratio h, cache time c and memory time m
Direct-mapped, fully associative and set-associative mapping, and how an address splits into [[tag, set or block, and word fields]]
Thrashing in a direct-mapped cache and how block size changes the hit ratio
Replacement policies: [[LRU, LFU, FIFO and random]]
Virtual memory: pages and frames, the page table and its control bits, page faults, swap space and the TLB
Page tables per process for protection, and how the page table size limits the number of processes that fit in RAM
do: Compute the number of tag, set and offset bits for a given cache and memory
Trace a sequence of accesses through a cache with LRU or LFU and count hits and misses
Compute hits, misses and the hit ratio of a loop over arrays for different mappings
Compute the size of a full page table from the RAM size, page size and control bits, rounded up to whole bytes or words
Say how many processes fit when each needs its own page table
pitfalls: Rounding page table entries wrongly: the entry is rounded up to the stated unit, which changes how many entries fit
Using a wrong cache or block size early on, which the rubrics penalise in every later part

topics.name: Pipelining and parallelism
know: Execution time [[T = N times S divided by R]], and how an n-stage pipeline divides it by up to n
The four-stage pipeline ([[Fetch, Decode, Execute, Writeback]]) with its interstage buffers
Stalls from cache misses, data dependencies, branches and long operations, and operand forwarding
Branch prediction, and the average extra cycles per instruction from miss rates and penalties
Latency versus throughput of a pipeline, and which stage limits it
Superscalar execution and out-of-order execution
Amdahl's law: [[Tp = Ts times (fs + fp / p)]], and the speedup it limits
Flynn's taxonomy ([[SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD]]), GPUs as SIMD, shared-memory multiprocessors and NUMA
do: Schedule an everyday multi-step process (printing an exam, releasing songs, streaming music) as a pipeline and compute its latency, throughput and number of workers needed
Compute the average extra clock cycles per instruction from instruction and data cache misses and branch mispredictions
Apply Amdahl's law forwards (speedup) and backwards (the parallel fraction from measured times)
Compare a many-core CPU with a slower GPU using Amdahl's law and find the break-even fraction
pitfalls: Forgetting that [[the slowest stage sets the throughput]] of a pipeline
Adding cache miss penalties without weighting them by how many instructions access data

prerequisites: None formally: the course starts in the first quarter of year 1
Comfort with powers of two and binary arithmetic without a calculator
Some programming experience helps for reading pseudocode and for the assembly lab
A Linux, WSL, virtual machine or Docker setup with GCC for the lab, which you prepare in week 1
practical: Three mandatory lab assignments in x86-64 assembly, done in pairs and signed off by a TA: Powers (a pow subroutine with input and output via scanf and printf), Recursion (factorial) and Memory (decoding a message stored as linked 8-byte blocks). They give no points but must be passed. Code must have a pseudocode specification, comments, stack frames for every subroutine and follow the calling convention. Eight bonus assignments (Assignments 4 to 11, 250 to 750 points) range from SHA-1 and printf to a Brainfuck interpreter and a game. Weekly self-study sets with peer review give 200 points each.
studyAdvice: Data representation and logic circuits together carry about a third of all exam points and fill most of each midterm. Drill radix conversions, signed formats, custom floating point, Karnaugh maps and CMOS until they are routine.

On the endterm side, caches and virtual memory, and pipelining with Amdahl's law, are about a quarter of the points. Practise hit and miss traces, page table sizes and pipeline schedules for everyday processes.
Do the assembly lab early and seriously: the last midterm question is usually an x86-64 stack trace, and it rewards the same stack frame habits the TAs check at sign-off.
Learn the microroutine notation (PC out, MAR in, READ, WMFC, END) by writing several microroutines yourself; every endterm and resit asks for one or for reading one.
Practise without a calculator: every paper is pen and paper with powers of two, conversions and small sums.
Do the weekly self-study sets: they cover each week's lectures in the exam style and give 200 points each, which can lift your grade.
Spend little time on the history lecture beyond the main machines, people and dates; it is one question of 200 to 300 points per midterm.
